newsitem.title: USA: Carroll O'Connor cleared in slander suit.
newsitem.headline: Carroll O'Connor cleared in slander suit.

text.p: A civil court jury on Friday cleared crusty character actor Carroll O'Connor of slander charges brought by a man O'Connor accused of helping to drive his son Hugh to suicide by supplying him with cocaine.
The verdict reached after 1-1/2 days of deliberations pleased the 72-year-old actor best known for his portrayal of TV's opinionated Archie Bunker.
O'Connor told Reuters: "I'm gratified" and said he felt free to continue to speak out against plaintiff Harry Perzigian because the jury "said it was okay and the jury is the boss."

Perzigian said, "I am disappointed obviously. You are never going to get a fair shake in this town. But I am glad I brought this case because it exhibited Carroll O'Connor as the hateful, vengeful person he is."

Members of the jury told reporters that they believed Perzigian did play a role in Hugh O'Connor's March 1995 suicide because he was a supplier of drugs to the troubled 32-year-old, who shot himself to death on his third wedding anniversary.
They added that Carroll O'Connor's celebrity status played no role in their deliberations.
Perzigian brought suit against O'Connor charging that the actor engaged in a malicious bid to avenge his son's suicide. He sought an apology and unspecified damages.

The jury also cleared the actor of charges of intentionally inflicting emotional distress on Perzigian, a songwriter who served a jail term for drug use and who has admitted occasionally giving cocaine to Hugh O'Connor.
Lawyers for O'Connor called Perzigian Hugh O'Connor's "cocaine connection" and portrayed him as a drug dealer, a charge he hotly denied.

In television interviews, Carroll O'Connor called Perzigian "a partner in murder" and "a lawbreaker." He also gave out his address and showed his photo. O'Connor said in one interview: "Harry Perzigian, you sleaze-ball. We're going to get you" and "I want to hurt him in the worst way."

In her closing argument, O'Connor's attorney, Lucy Inman, told the jury to consider the comments as from a grieving father who had lost his only son and to view the case as a blow in the battle against drugs.
Perzigian's lawyer, Allan Sigel, called the case a David versus Goliath battle but said his client was not responsible for Hugh O'Connor's death.
